headlines.article_text: Eli Lilly (LLY) earnings Q3 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Eli Lilly reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook. Demand for its obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro surged again and topped estimates for the quarter. Despite that strength, sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo, which launched in the U.S. in April, were under Wall Street's expectations for the quarter. In this article LLY Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:53 04:53 Eli Lilly CEO Dave Ricks on the obesity market: The room for expansion is dramatic Squawk on the Street Eli Lilly on Thursday reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past estimates and hiked its full-year sales outlook, as demand for its blockbuster weight loss drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro soared again. Despite that strength, sales of its new GLP-1 obesity pill Foundayo, which launched in the U.S. in April, were under Wall Street's expectations for the quarter. The pharmaceutical giant now expects 2026 revenue to come in between $91 billion and $92 billion, up from a previous guidance of $85 billion to $87 billion. Lilly projects its full-year adjusted earnings will be between $35 and $36 per share, which compares with a previous outlook of $35.50 to $36.50 per share. The company said it raised the underlying profit guidance by $4.07 per share at the midpoint, but noted that it is offset by $4.57 per share in charges tied to deals in the quarter. The company's shares rose about 9% on Thursday. Lilly's massive diabetes and obesity windfall – and market share lead over chief rival Novo – shows no signs of slowing down, even as the company grapples with lower net prices in the U.S. The pharma giant is converting its massive profits into a dealmaking spree, most recently striking an agreement to buy Merida Biosciences to develop a new class of treatments for serious autoimmune and allergic diseases. Here's what Eli Lilly reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $7.48 adjusted vs. $6.26 expected Revenue: $24.40 billion vs. $22.61 billion expected Resilient demand for Zepbound and Mounjaro has helped fuel several strong quarters for Lilly despite lower prices for the medications in the U.S., which came after a drug pricing deal struck with the Trump administration last year. In a release, Lilly also pointed to expanded U.S. coverage for obesity care, referring to Medicare's decision to start covering GLP-1s for weight loss in July under a temporary pilot program. "This is a program that's really working," Lilly CEO Dave Ricks said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We're pleased with the early uptake and access, and I think doctors and patients are as well." Mounjaro's worldwide revenue rose 65% to $10.72 billion for the quarter, including U.S. sales of about $5 billion. That surpassed the $10.10 billion in worldwide sales and $4.79 billion in U.S. revenue that analysts were expecting for the quarter, according to StreetAccount. Mounjaro notably saw strength internationally, with sales outside the U.S. jumping 93%. Zepbound, which entered the market roughly three years ago, posted $5.35 billion in revenue for the third quarter. That's up 49% from the year-earlier period, as demand for the drug also rose while realized prices dropped. The vast majority of those sales came from the U.S. Analysts were expecting $5.09 billion in global sales for Zepbound, including $4.99 billion from the U.S., according to StreetAccount. The Eli Lilly logo appears on the company’s office in San Diego, California, Nov. 21, 2025. Mike Blake | Reuters Lilly's newly launched obesity pill, Foundayo, which won U.S. approval in April, took in $184 million in sales for the third quarter. That fell under analyst forecasts of around $229 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates showed. It marks the second earnings report that includes revenue from the GLP-1 pill, which is competing head-to-head with a rival oral drug from Novo that launched in January. Total U.S. prescriptions for Foundayo and the number of new Foundayo patients in the third quarter doubled from the previous quarter, Lilly CFO Lucas Montarces said during a Thursday earnings call. Around 4 in 10 patients starting an oral obesity medicine choose Foundayo, he added. Lilly expects Foundayo to win U.S. approval for Type 2 diabetes in the fourth quarter. Lilly is working to maintain its dominance in the booming market for GLP-1 drugs, with the company holding 63% share of the U.S. obesity and diabetes drug market in the third quarter, according to an earnings presentation on Thursday. Novo's market share in the quarter was 36.6%. During the earnings call, Montarces said 7 out of 10 U.S. prescriptions for injectable obesity and diabetes drugs in the third quarter were for a Lilly medicine. Ricks told CNBC that he estimates 3% to 10% of eligible patients access obesity care in the U.S., but said the "room for expansion here of this market is dramatic." Lilly is at the front of that push, he added. Internationally, Lilly held 58.4% share of the market, while Novo had 41.6%, the presentation said. Eli Lilly's revenue in the U.S. climbed 34% to $15.1 billion. Lilly said it saw a 41% increase in volume — or the number of prescriptions or units sold — for its products, primarily for Mounjaro and Zepbound. That was partially offset by a 7% decrease in realized prices, primarily driven by Zepbound. Lilly's quarter was also boosted by a sales-based milestone payout of $410 million for its Type 2 diabetes medication Jardiance, related to the company's collaboration with Boehringer Ingelheim. Sales outside the U.S. jumped 47% to $9.3 billion, propelled by a 76% surge in volume and partly offset by a 29% drop in realized prices. The pharmaceutical giant booked net income of $6.45 billion, or $7.22 per share, for the third quarter, which includes the $4.57 per share deal charges. That compares with net income of $5.58 billion, or $6.21 per share, a year earlier. Excluding one-time items associated with the value of intangible assets and other adjustments, Eli Lilly posted earnings of $7.48 per share for the third quarter. headlines.article_text: Alphabet earnings miss first sign AI is taking a bite out of search Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Wall Street hammered Alphabet for an earnings miss that included weaker-than-expected revenue in the company's core business. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. Regarding new AI agents and bots, Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said, "These things are going to be a force." In this article GOOGL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Sundar Pichai, CEO of Alphabet, during the Google I/O Developers Conference in Mountain View, California, May 19, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images In Alphabet's across-the-board earnings miss , one segment stood out above all else: search. Revenue in the search and other segment grew 12% from a year ago to roughly $63 billion, but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. At the same time, Google said search query growth on the platform was the strongest it's been in five years. The gap between usage and revenue within the search giant's flagship business is becoming harder to dismiss as more people turn to artificial intelligence bots and agents, including tools offered by Google. Since the early days of ChatGPT, analysts have predicted that traditional search will get eclipsed by AI, and warned that Google will have to figure out new ways to make money. While search remains a massive business, early signs of a shift are appearing. "These things are going to be a force," Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster told CNBC's " Fast Money " after the earnings report, referring to new AI-powered services. Munster said that if "personalized bots" take off, "that will become for a lot of people the starting point of commerce, which impacts where Google is." watch now VIDEO 5:16 05:16 AI search queries hurt Alphabet's core business, says Deepwater's Gene Munster Fast Money Alphabet executives said foreign exchange was the biggest factor behind the deceleration in search revenue in the period, and said the currency impact would be even greater in the fourth quarter. The stock plummeted about 10% in extended trading, reflecting the weaker-than-expected earnings report and negative free cash flow of $9 billion for the quarter, three times the estimated deficit. In the second quarter, Alphabet's free cash flow went negative for the first time in its history as a public company, at $5.9 billion. Google has spent much of the past year telling investors that it needs to pour money into AI infrastructure and services to meet unending demand from consumers and businesses. Google's Gemini model has allowed the company to stay competitive with Anthropic and OpenAI , and its Gemini-powered enterprise services have proven to be a hit with customers. The company also says that Gemini is strengthening its core digital ads business, as it uses AI to improve its ability to understand user intent and make advertising more relevant. “We continue to accelerate the deployment of Gemini models across our entire ads infrastructure to boost performance,” Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler said on the third-quarter earnings call. Read more CNBC tech news AI build-out hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search As Waymo expands overseas, it remains a niche cash-burning business Hands-on with Apple’s first touchscreen laptop: Touch is totally optional The company made what Schindler called its “biggest update to product listing ads in a decade” during the third quarter, adding new AI capabilities. “Overall, AI is accelerating our ads development and drives the majority of our product launches,” Schindler said. Advertisers are also rapidly adopting AI tools. In the third quarter, Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier, Schindler said. But none of that addresses revenue growth for search, which slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, before falling to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote in a note that the results are "going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront." And Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers are an issue for search and YouTube. "This elevates the fear around AI and agentic taking share from Search and YT and hurting their AI monetization narrative," Klein wrote in a note after the earnings report. Cloud gives Alphabet its AI payoff Where Alphabet's AI bet is very much paying off is in its cloud business. Revenue in that division, which is racing to catch up to Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion. Cloud backlog also reached roughly $560 billion, reflecting enormous contracted demand for AI infrastructure. Management said it expects just more than half of that backlog to be recognized over the next 24 months. In Microsoft's quarterly earnings report , which also landed after the bell Wednesday, the software maker said Azure revenue increased 48% from a year earlier to $33.2 billion. Cloud demand is a big reason for Alphabet to keep spending. The company maintained its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast of $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will increase significantly in 2027. Some of that is for its tensor processing units , or TPUs, which compete with Nvidia's graphics processing units. Alphabet just started selling them to outside customers in the second quarter. Google released its 7th generation TPU, Ironwood, in November 2025, a decade after making its first custom ASIC for AI in 2015. Google Customer agreements first show up in Google Cloud’s backlog, and the company has to spend money building the systems before it can deliver them and recognize the associated revenue. “You see cash going out and we’re building up the inventory base,” Alphabet CFO Anat Ashkenazi said on the earnings call. “As we start delivering and billing customers for these TPU systems, then you see cash coming in.” Still, Google has to contend with concerns about its longtime cash cow. Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, said the fears that existed from 2023 to 2025 about the AI effect appear to finally be showing up in Google's business. "Investors will now worry that the miss in Search, YouTube and Subscription, leading to a profit miss, are an indication that AI has finally come for Google," Luria wrote in an email. "We would not rush to conclusions based on one quarter, but will definitely need to reassess what the world of agentic commerce means for Google." headlines.article_text: Restaurant Brands International (QSR) Q3 2026 earnings Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Restaurant Brands International reported better-than-expected quarterly earnings, but its revenue fell slightly short of Wall Street's expectations. Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. Popeyes U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%, making it the weakest chain in Restaurant Brands' portfolio. In this article QSR Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT In this photo illustration, a Burger King Whopper and fries are seen in a restaurant on August 17, 2026, in Hollywood, Florida. Joe Raedle | Getty Images Restaurant Brands International on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as Popeyes' struggles offset Burger King's successful U.S. turnaround . Shares of the company fell about 1% in morning trading. Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: $1.10 adjusted vs. $1.09 expected Revenue: $2.53 billion vs. $2.54 billion expected Restaurant Brands reported third-quarter net income attributable to common shareholders of $542 million, or $1.54 per share, up from $315 million, or 96 cents per share, a year earlier. Excluding certain noncash items, the company earned $1.10 per share. Net revenue rose 3.1% to $2.53 billion. Across all of its restaurants, the company reported same-store sales growth of 3.8%. Restaurant Brands has reported same-store sales growth above 3% for the past five quarters. Burger King was the top performer, with U.S. same-store sales growth of 8.4%. The burger chain's home market is in the middle of multiyear turnaround, with a focus on improving its food and restaurants. "The plans we've put in place over the last several years are working, and we're going to keep executing against them," Restaurant Brands Chair Patrick Doyle said on the company's earnings conference call. "Burger King has delivered over four years of industry outperformance, and now we've seen three consecutive quarters of truly exceptional results." Tim Hortons reported same-store sales growth of 1.8% in Canada, its home market. In July, the coffee chain launched a line of matcha drinks, bringing more customers to its locations during the sleepier afternoon hours. Popeyes was once again the laggard of Restaurant Brands' portfolio. The fried chicken chain's U.S. same-store sales fell 2.2%. In recent quarters, Popeyes has struggled as other chicken rivals have lured its customers away with discounts. Restaurant Brands is trying to stage a comeback with improved restaurant operations and a focus on its core menu. Restaurant Brands previously forecast that Popeyes would return to same-store sales growth in the second half of 2026, but CEO Josh Kobza said on the earnings call that the company now believes it will take longer, although traffic is improving. The return of Popeyes' $6 Big Box promotion in September boosted sales less than expected, according to Kobza. Plus, the chain has scaled back its wings to refocus on its core menu items, hurting sales in the short term. The company's international business saw same-store sales growth of 3.9%, fueled by its Burger King locations. DoorDash will pay $65 a share in cash and stock, an 11% premium to Instacart's closing price on Wednesday, and about 26% above Instacart's closing price on Oct. 22, the last trading day before reports surfaced of a possible sale. Shares of DoorDash jumped more than 8% in premarket trading following news of the deal, while Instacart traded near the flatline. The deal is slated to close at the end of 2027 or early 2028, the companies said. DoorDash expects to retain Instacart's brand, enterprise technology products and app once the deal closes. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in a statement that grocery is "one of the hardest things to get right online." He pointed to difficulties around picking the right inventory and delivering perishable goods to customers' doorsteps without damaging them on the way. "Instacart has spent years learning to do that well for grocers, while DoorDash has built a delivery network and technology that local stores rely on every day," Xu said. "Together, we could give stores of every size more of those tools and unlock the potential of grocery delivery." Adjusted earnings per share were $1.06, beating the average analyst estimate of 84 cents per share, according to LSEG. Revenue came in at $4.62 billion, topping LSEG estimates of $4.56 billion. Marketplace gross order value, which tracks the total dollar value of orders on its platform, grew 36% year over year to $33.9 billion, beating consensus estimates of $33.6 billion. Total orders reached 993 million, up 28% from a year ago. Speculation of a deal has swirled since last week, when The Information reported Instacart was exploring a sale and had held talks with companies including Uber and DoorDash. On Monday, several outlets reported DoorDash was in advanced discussions to acquire Instacart and that the deal could value Instacart at about $17 billion. Sources familiar with the matter had told CNBC on Wednesday that the deal could be announced as soon as Thursday morning. Acquiring Instacart would give DoorDash a bigger presence in online grocery delivery. DoorDash got its start in food delivery, and since then, it has added more retailers to its marketplace, such as Sephora, Macy's , Staples and Anthropologie. It's recently made grocery a bigger priority, adding a stable of regional grocers after announcing a partnership with Kroger last year. Instacart , which went public in 2023, was one of the biggest beneficiaries of a pandemic-driven surge in grocery delivery services, but it has struggled to maintain that momentum. headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: Alphabet, Caterpillar, Eli Lilly, DoorDash & more
headlines.summary: These are the stocks posting the largest moves in the premarket.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: GOOGL, CAT, LLY, DASH Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves in premarket trading: Alphabet — The Google parent dropped 11% after its third-quarter earnings showed the company posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion. Its core search revenue of $63.35 billion missed the $64.96 billion estimate from analysts. Total company revenue of $127.58 billion also missed LSEG expectations of $128.22 billion. Caterpillar — Shares slid 9% even after the company reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that beat the Street. The company earned an adjusted $7.20 per share on revenue of $20.68 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG expected a profit of $7.08 per share on revenue of $20.55 billion. However, sales for its construction industries business came in slightly below estimates. DoorDash , Maplebear — DoorDash announced it is acquiring the Instacart parent for $65 per share. That is an 11% premium from Maplebear's closing price on Wednesday. DoorDash also reported a revenue and EBITDA beat for its third quarter. Maplebear was up 4.8% before trading was halted, while DoorDash rose 7%. Eli Lilly — The Zepbound and Mounjaro maker handily beat expectations for its third quarter, sending shares 4% higher. Eli Lilly saw adjusted earnings of $7.48 per share, compared with the consensus estimate $6.26 a share, per LSEG. Revenue came in at $24.4 billion, topping the $22.61 billion expected from analysts. Marvell Technology , Lumentum — Lumentum shares jumped 5% after Bloomberg News reported, citing sources that the data center optics manufacturer was in talks to be acquired by Marvell. A deal could be announced as soon as next week, the report said . Marvell shares dropped more than 11%. Microsoft — The software giant rose 2% after the company reported a beat on the top and bottom lines for its fiscal first-quarter earnings. Revenue came in at $92.28 billion, ahead of the $90.69 billion expected by LSEG. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share was better than the $4.73 expected by analysts. Revenue in the mega-cap's key Azure cloud business grew 48% year over year. Shell — The oil major climbed 3.6% after it nearly doubled its third-quarter profit from the year prior to $10.81 billion. Analysts polled by LSEG were expecting $9.92 billion. Norwegian Cruise Line — The cruise operator jumped 9.5% following its beat on the top and bottom lines. Norwegian reported adjusted earnings of $1.12 per share, topping the consensus estimate of 93 cents, according to FactSet. Revenue was $2.95 billion, versus the $2.88 billion anticipated by analysts. Chipotle Mexican Grill — Shares gained nearly 8% after the burrito chain reported same-store sales that beat estimates. Same-store sales in the third quarter grew 2.1%, versus the 1.5% increase analysts polled by FactSet anticipated. ServiceNow — The enterprise software company tumbled 20%. Third-quarter adjusted profit of $1 per share missed the LSEG consensus expectation of $1.02 a share. Subscription revenue guidance for the fourth quarter ranged from $4.245 billion to $4.255 billion, while the FactSet consensus called for $4.25 billion. Fortinet — The cybersecurity company plummeted 25.5%. Non-GAAP gross margin for the third quarter came in at 79.6%, while analysts polled by LSEG sought 80.1%. Separately, top and bottom-line results beat the Street's expectations. Sprouts Farmers Market — The Phoenix-based grocery chain plunged 23% after third-quarter earnings per share, revenue and same-store sales all trailed analysts' consensus estimates, according to FactSet data. Harley-Davidson — Shares of the motorcycle maker dropped 5% following a revenue miss in its latest quarter. Harley-Davidson posted revenue of $964.0 million, falling short of the StreetAccount consensus estimate of $1.07 billion. On the other hand, adjusted EBITDA of $93.9 million topped the FactSet consensus of $78.9 million. Crocs — The footwear stock surged nearly 18% after Crocs posted third-quarter earnings that beat expectations, and issued stronger-than-expected current quarter guidance. It posted earnings of $3.69 per share, excluding items, on revenue of $1.04 billion. Analysts polled by FactSet anticipated earnings of $3.31 per share on revenue of $1.00 billion. eBay — Shares climbed more than 6% after the company reported stronger-than-expected third-quarter results. Revenue rose 14% to $3.2 billion, while gross merchandise volume increased 15%. Growth from Depop, accelerating GMV, and raised full-year guidance gave investors further confidence in eBay's strategy. Honeywell Aerospace — The aerospace company was down 4% even after raising its full-year outlook for pro forma standalone adjusted earnings per share, calling for $7.85 to $8. The company also announced an initial quarterly cash dividend of 40 cents per share. Carvana — The used car dealer climbed 8%. Carvana third-quarter revenue and adjusted EBITDA topped the numbers Wall Street had been expecting, and it said the Securities and Exchange Commission closed a previously disclosed investigation and would not take any enforcement action. CNBC's Darla Mercado, Fred Imbert, Sarah Min, Paulina Likos, Scott Schnipper, Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells contributed reporting.
